It is quite clear that, in the long run, any serious attention-getting scheme will be unpalatable and, as it is impossible to dissuade the public, it will finally be rejected. The new and much talked of scheme for the production of a national consciousness, by means of a public school-system, which, by introducing the element of discipline into childhood, will make the mass more tractable and obedient and will render the individual more amenable to discipline and obedience, has failed to attract the attention of the public. But this may not be a bad thing.

In the same way, the attention-getting system of the stage is a failure. The public does not care about it. The audiences of the past were more numerous than they are today, and the theatres were filled; the audiences of the present are smaller than they used to be; the theatres are half empty. The great attention-getting devices of the stage, the use of the chorus, the soliloquy, the introduction of song and dance, the use of stage pictures, the use of fireworks and the like, are no longer appreciated. The modern play-goer has a much clearer and keener and more discerning intelligence than the one of the past, and he is less able to be hypnotized or goaded or driven into paying attention by any contrivances of art. The modern play-goer has a much higher standard of appreciation than the one of the past, and he is less able to be made to think of something other than what the play is intended to show. The modern play-goer does not care to be addressed, and he does not care to have his attention fixed upon him. He does not care to hear the words, the voice, or the music of the play. He cares for the play itself. He does not care to see a stage show, with a chorus and a choir, with a band and a drum corps, with a crowd of actors, a crowd of singers, a crowd of dancers, and a crowd of musicians, all playing and singing and dancing and shouting and roaring and making a din in the most unholy manner; he cares for the story. He does not care for any kind of artifice which takes away from the play what is best in it, and he does not care to have his attention attracted to anything which is not a part of the play.
